title: LCIA Challenge Decision — Decision 10 (10/05/2019)
text:
DECISION RENDERED ON 10 MAY 2019
Subject: The Claimants challenged the Sole Arbitrator (selected by the LCIA Court)
pursuant to Article 10.3 of the LCIA Rules 2014.
Outcome: Rejected
Seat: London, England
Governing Law of English law
the Contract:
Summary: The challenge related, among other things, to the Sole Arbitrator’s: (i)
appointment by the LCIA Court – consisting of a Vice-President who has been
a member for a number of years and who will soon be promoted to
President – while that same Vice-President remains a partner at the law firm
representing the Respondents; (ii) Order for Security; (iii) Partial Final Award;
(iv) Award on Wasted Costs; and (v) decision on hearing location.
The LCIA Court rejected the challenge.
The LCIA Court considered the challenge on the basis of the LCIA Rules,
together with the English Arbitration Act 1996 (the law of the seat), as
relevant.
The LCIA Court accepted, for the purposes of determining whether the
challenge was timely, that the Claimants only learned of the Vice-President’s
promotion to President of the LCIA Court recently after the filing of the
challenge, even though the promotion was announced some time before.
While other circumstances invoked by the Claimants occurred outside of the
14-day period (e.g. the Vice-President’s earlier role on the LCIA Court and the
LCIA Board, the Vice-President’s membership of the LCIA, a related court
action also involving the Vice-President’s law firm), the LCIA Court
considered the Claimants' concerns about these circumstances to have
accumulated in the appointment of the Vice-President as President of the
LCIA Court and therefore deemed the challenge on this ground to be timely.
The Vice-President’s upcoming new role on the LCIA Court, including the
current roles on the LCIA Court and the LCIA Board, do not give rise to
justifiable doubts as to the Sole Arbitrator's impartiality or independence.
There was no evidence or basis for an impression that the LCIA Court had
appointed the Sole Arbitrator under the instruction of the Vice-President or
under the direction of the Vice-President’s law firm. Regardless, the
Constitution of the LCIA Court prohibits any involvement by the Vice-

President under the circumstances. The Vice-President cannot be equated
with the LCIA Court as a whole; the Sole Arbitrator cannot be equated with
the interests or position of the Vice-President or the Respondents. The LCIA
Court is also not under the direction and control of the Vice-President’s law
firm (and Respondents’ counsel), and the LCIA Court is not (and cannot be
analogised to) a legal representative of the Respondents.
The fact that the Vice-President’s law firm also acts for one Respondent in
court proceedings against one Claimant, which include fraud allegations
against that Claimant, does not change the analysis.
The Claimants objected to the Sole Arbitrator’s Order for Security less than
14 days after it was issued, but the challenge was filed more than 14 days
after the Order. Since the challenge largely repeated the objections made
within the deadline, the LCIA Court accepted that the allegations relating to
the Order were timely.
The Claimants’ allegation that the Sole Arbitrator’s Order for Security was
based on a “misinterpretation” of the Claimants’ submissions had no merit.
Even if the Sole Arbitrator stated that non-payment of previous costs
awarded against the Claimants was the result of “tactical and commercial”
considerations, whereas the Claimants had indicated in their submissions
that non-payment was for “practical and commercial reasons” rather than
“tactical” reasons, a fair-minded observer would conclude that there was an
innocent misunderstanding or miscommunication, in particular given the
similarity between the words “practical” and “tactical”.
While the Claimants may disagree with the Order for Security, this is not a
valid basis to challenge the Sole Arbitrator. The amount ordered as security
was calculated on the basis of submissions received from the Parties and
reasoned in the Order. It was not without basis and it was not oppressive in
the sense of attempting to stifle the Claimants’ claims. Moreover, the
Claimants have not established that compliance with the Order for Security
was a precondition for continuing with their claims, that non-compliance
necessarily entailed dismissal of their claims, or that they were forced to
withdraw their claims if they could not comply. The Order for Security did
not address any consequences of noncompliance.
The challenge is not the appropriate forum to consider the Claimants’
complaints relating to the Sole Arbitrator’s conclusions in the Partial Final
Award. The Claimants’ allegation that the Partial Final Award included
damages, even though, according to the Claimants, the proceedings had
been bifurcated between liability and quantum, has no merit. The Sole
Arbitrator understood the Parties had agreed to bifurcate only with respect
to the Claimants’ claims, not the Respondents’ counterclaim, and the Sole
Arbitrator’s reading of the Parties’ agreement does not give rise to justifiable
Decision 10 - 2

doubts as to impartiality or independence. To the extent the Claimants
invoke lack of due process, the circumstances do not reveal any failure to act
fairly or impartially as between the Parties. The Sole Arbitrator gave all
Parties the opportunity to present their claims and evidence.
The fact that the Sole Arbitrator had expressed a “strong tentative view” that
the question of costs be deferred until the end of the arbitration, while
ultimately deciding to receive submissions and render an award on wasted
costs during the proceedings, does not support an allegation of bias. A
tentative view is a preliminary one, even if strongly held, and is not
definitive. In any event, a change in view as to the most appropriate manner
of conducting the proceedings, in particular after receiving both Parties'
comments, does not raise concerns as to an arbitrator's impartiality or
independence.
The Sole Arbitrator’s decision to move the hearing venue from London to
New York, upon the Claimants’ own application that the hearing be moved
to either Miami or New York (in light of one Claimant’s alleged inability to
travel outside of the United States), does not support an allegation of bias.
The fact that the Claimants preferred Miami and the Respondents preferred
New York and that the Sole Arbitrator tentatively expressed a view in favour
of Miami does not give rise to justifiable doubts as to impartiality or
independence.
The LCIA Court is not competent to determine the Sole Arbitrator’s
jurisdiction or the validity of any award.
The above circumstances, considered as a whole, do not give rise to
justifiable doubts as to the Sole Arbitrator’s impartiality or independence.
Decision 10 - 3

DECISION ON THE CHALLENGE OF THE SOLE ARBITRATOR
____________________________________________
10 MAY 2019
I. PROCEDURE
1. On 7 November 2017, the LCIA Court appointed [A] as sole arbitrator in LCIA Case No. […] (“the Sole
Arbitrator”).
2. On 2 May 2018, the Sole Arbitrator rendered an Award on Jurisdiction (“Award on Jurisdiction”).
3. On 20 September 2018, the Sole Arbitrator rendered an Award on Costs of the Jurisdiction Award
(“Award on Costs re Jurisdiction Award”).
4. On 29 October 2018, the Sole Arbitrator rendered an Award on Costs of 2nd and 3rd Respondents
Wasted/Thrown Away in Dealing with Claimants’ Pleadings (“Award on Wasted Costs”).
1 First Respondent has not participated in the arbitration to date. References to “Respondents” herein
therefore refer to Second and Third Respondents jointly, to the exclusion of First Respondent.
Decision 10 - 4

5. On 4 January 2019, the Sole Arbitrator issued an order for both Claimants and Second Respondent to
put up security for costs (“Order for Security”). On 5 January 2019, the Sole Arbitrator amended the
Order for Security with respect to the amount ordered.
6. On 15 January 2019, Claimants addressed a letter to the Sole Arbitrator (“Claimants’ Letter of 15
January 2019”), stating among other things as follows:
The purpose of this letter is to set out three serious complaints with the way this arbitration
has been conducted by the Tribunal, which have caused serious and irreparable prejudice to
the Claimants so that they have been unable to fairly present their case. Due to these fatal
defects, the Claimants are forced to withdraw their claims.2
7. In their Letter of 15 January 2019, Claimants detailed their submissions that (i) the order directing
payment of USD 1.25 million security for costs within 7 business days is based on a misinterpretation
of the Claimants’ argument and the facts, is unduly oppressive, and the Claimants lack any ability to
comply; (ii) the LCIA and the Sole Arbitrator are biased and partial against Claimants and have acted
in such a way as to cause serious prejudice to Claimants; (iii) in any event, the Sole Arbitrator has no
jurisdiction to decide Second Respondent’s counterclaims against Second Claimant; and (iv) due to
lack of fairness in the process, Claimants are forced to withdraw their claims.
8. On 18 January 2019, Respondents replied to Claimants’ letter of 15 January 2019, submitting that
Claimants’ complaints are “extraordinary, unsubstantiated and entirely without merit” and
responding to each complaint in turn (“Respondents’ Letter of 18 January 2019”).3
9. On 25 January 2019, Claimants addressed a letter to the President of the LCIA Court (“Claimants’
Letter of 25 January 2019”), submitting that:
violations of mandatory standards of conduct committed by the Tribunal and the London
Court of International Arbitration . . . have caused serious and irreparable prejudice to the
Claimants so that they have been unable to present their case.4
10. Referring to and repeating the complaints made in their letter of 15 January 2019, Claimants
requested that the LCIA Court “recuse the arbitrator and then recuse itself from conducting this
2 Claimants’ Letter of 15 January 2019, p. 1.
3 Second and Third Respondents’ Letter of 18 January 2019, p. 1.
4 Claimants’ Letter of 25 January 2019, p. 1.
Decision 10 - 5

arbitration because an impartial observer would conclude that the LCIA Court and the Tribunal are
biased against the Claimants”.5
11. On 28 January 2019, the LCIA Secretariat acknowledged receipt of Claimants’ letter dated 25 January
2019, including the request for the LCIA Court to “recuse the arbitrator and then recuse itself from
conducting this arbitration”. The LCIA requested Claimants to confirm whether their letter of 25
January 2019 represents a challenge to the Sole Arbitrator under Article 10.1 of the LCIA Arbitration
Rules effective 1 October 2014 (“LCIA Rules”) and therefore should be decided by the LCIA Court
pursuant to Article 10.6 of the LCIA Rules.
12. On 1 February 2019, the Sole Arbitrator replied as follows to Claimants’ Letter of 25 January 2019:
Although that letter is addressed to […], I note that it suggest that I should recuse myself.
I do not propose to engage with the allegations made in that letter. I think it would be
inappropriate to do.
However, for the sake of good order, I should say that I do not consider that there is any
basis for the allegations; that I will not recuse myself; and that the hearing will proceed next
week as previously ordered.
13. On 1 February 2019, Claimants replied to the LCIA Secretariat’s email of 28 January 2019, stating as
follows:
For the reasons stated in our letter dated 25 January 2019, the Claimants’ position is that
the LCIA Court lacks the necessary impartiality and independence to conduct this arbitration,
including but not limited to, considering a challenge to the impartiality of the arbitrator in
this case, and that the LCIA Court should recuse itself from conducting or overseeing this
arbitration. For the avoidance of any doubt, Claimants are challenging the impartiality of the
arbitrator, and are also challenging the impartiality of the LCIA Court, and are thus
requesting that the LCIA Court recuse itself from conducting any and all aspects of this
arbitration. Should the LCIA Court proceed to administer the arbitration under these
circumstances, Claimants believe that an impartial observer would conclude that the LCIA
Court is biased against Claimants. To the extent that the LCIA Court refuses to recuse itself,
and should the LCIA Court decide to proceed to administer the arbitration notwithstanding
Claimants’ pleas to the contrary, Claimants would direct the LCIA Court to consider
Claimants’ challenge of the sole arbitrator for the reasons stated in the 25 January 2019
letter.
5 Ibid., pp. 1-2.
Decision 10 - 6

14. In a separate email to the Sole Arbitrator on 1 February 2019, Claimants reiterated that they had
withdrawn their claims without prejudice. In the absence of any “dispute, controversy or claim”, and
relying on English legal authorities, Claimants submitted that the Sole Arbitrator has no jurisdiction.
Claimants further requested (i) confirmation that the Phase I hearing will not proceed; and (ii) an
order confirming that Claimants’ claims have been withdrawn and no final award will be issued on
Claimants’ claims.
15. On 2 February 2019, the Sole Arbitrator requested Claimants to file copies of the authorities referred
to in their email of 1 February 2019.
16. On 4 February 2019, Claimants submitted copies of the two legal authorities referred to in their
email of 1 February 2019.
17. On 5 February 2019, the Sole Arbitrator stated that he was unable to provide the confirmation that
Claimants requested in their email of 1 February 2019, although:
I will of course consider the points you raise as well as any submissions that may be made on
behalf of the Second and Third Respondents in the course of the hearing commencing
tomorrow 6 February 2019. Thereafter, I shall make such determination as may be
appropriate by way of an award or otherwise.
18. On 5 February 2019, the LCIA Secretariat addressed the Parties as follows:
Having consulted the LCIA Court, we inform the parties that the LCIA will not recuse itself
from administering the arbitration. We bring to the parties’ attention that it is not for the
LCIA to recuse itself in the event one of the parties in the arbitration raises a challenge to the
Tribunal under Article 10 of the Rules.
We understand the Claimants’ email of 1 February 2019 as the request for the LCIA Court to
determine the challenge under Article 10.
We understand from the Respondents’ letter of 18 January 2019 that the Second and Third
Respondents do not agree to the challenge. We also understand from the Sole Arbitrators’
[sic] email of 1 February 2019 that he does not agree to resign. If the Second and Third
Respondents and/or the Sole Arbitrator have any additional comments to the challenge
would they please provide them within 10 days, i.e. by Friday, 15 February 2019.
19. On 6 February 2019, a hearing was held, attended by the Sole Arbitrator and Respondents.
Claimants were not represented at the hearing.
Decision 10 - 7

20. Also on 6 February 2019, the LCIA Secretariat wrote to the Parties:
In light of my email [of 5 February 2019] and for the interest of clarity, subject to prompt
comments from the Respondents and the Sole Arbitrator, we understand that their position
stands as indicated below, namely that the Second and Third Respondents do not agree with
the challenge and the Sole Arbitrator is not inclined to resign. Pursuant to Article 10.6 the
LCIA Court shall proceed to decide the challenge.
The deadline for comments in response to the challenge, if any, remains the same, namely
15 February 2019.
21. On 8 February 2019, Claimants made further comments in relation to the English legal authorities on
the issue of the discontinuance of arbitration proceedings. Claimants maintained their position that
they were forced to withdraw their claims due to the “unlawful and absolutely impermissible conflict
of interest that permeates the LCIA”. Noting that the LCIA has rejected its own recusal, Claimants
submitted that at a minimum, [Law Firm D] should be required to desist from representation of
Respondents.
22. On 15 February 2019, Respondents requested that the LCIA Court dismiss Claimants’ application to
remove the Sole Arbitrator, and detailed certain comments in relation to the challenge
(“Respondents’ Email of 15 February 2019”).
23. On 18 February 2019, in correspondence following up from the hearing of 6 February 2019,
Claimants responded to an invitation from the Sole Arbitrator to provide any comments in relation
to certain interest calculations. In those comments, Claimants contended, among other things, that
(i) they were forced to withdraw their claims due to the unlawful and irreconcilable conflict of
interest that permeates the LCIA; (ii) the LCIA refused to recuse itself without any explanation and
before hearing Respondents’ position; and (iii) the LCIA’s position renders the arbitration clause
incapable of being performed, thereby affecting the validity of any award.
24. On 19 February 2019, the LCIA Court appointed [B] to decide upon the challenge to the Sole
Arbitrator […] (“the Undersigned”).
25. On 21 February 2019, the Undersigned set a procedural timetable to provide the Parties and the
Sole Arbitrator with the opportunity to comment upon the challenge, pursuant to Article 10.4 of the
LCIA Rules, and to present any further submissions or evidence. The Undersigned further requested
Claimants to submit copies of certain documents from the record.
Decision 10 - 8

26. On 1 March 2019, Claimants ratified and reasserted the positions taken in their correspondence of
15 January 2019, 25 January 2019, 1 February 2019, 8 February 2019 and 18 February 2019
(together referred to in this Decision as the “Challenge”) (“Claimants’ Email of 1 March 2019”).
Claimants also filed three exhibits in support of their Challenge, and stated that:
The Claimants have raised other issues regarding the arbitral institution that is administering
this arbitration, but the Claimants understand that such issues do not fall within the scope of
your mandate. (The LCIA has already stated that there is no mechanism for recusal of the
LCIA as the administrator of the arbitration)
27. On 4 March 2019, the Sole Arbitrator filed comments on the Challenge, together with four
attachments (“Sole Arbitrator’s Email of 4 March 2019”).
28. On 7 March 2019, Respondents submitted their comments on the Challenge, together with a bundle
of documents (“Respondents’ Letter of 7 March 2019”).
29. On 18 March 2019, the Sole Arbitrator rendered a Partial Final Award making a number of decisions,
including an order that “all of the Claimants’ claims are hereby rejected and dismissed”, and
ordering Claimants to pay certain amounts to Second Respondent.6
30. On 21 March 2019, following a request for extension of time which was granted by the Undersigned,
Claimants filed their reply comments on the Challenge, with four exhibits (“Claimants’ Letter of 21
March 2019”).
31. On 22 March 2019, the Sole Arbitrator submitted his rejoinder comments on the Challenge (“Sole
Arbitrator’s Email of 22 March 2019”).
32. On 28 March 2019, Respondents indicated that they did not intend to file any further submissions on
the Challenge, but concurred with the Sole Arbitrator’s Email of 22 March 2019.
33. No comments on the Challenge were received from First Respondent, which has not participated in
the arbitration proceedings to date.
34. In Section II below, the Undersigned will set out the legal standard relevant to the determination of
the Challenge. Section III contains the analysis of each ground, including the facts relevant to the
6 Exhibit 3, Claimants’ Letter of 21 March 2019.
Decision 10 - 9

Challenge, the Parties’ and the Sole Arbitrator’s positions, and the determination with respect to
each ground for the Challenge.
II. LEGAL STANDARD
35. It is undisputed that the LCIA Rules are the procedural rules applicable in this matter and that
London is the legal seat of these proceedings.7 The Undersigned will accordingly consider the
Challenge on the basis of the LCIA Rules, together with the English Arbitration Act 1996 (“Arbitration
Act”), as relevant.
36. Article 10 of the LCIA Rules provides as follows:
10.1 The LCIA Court may revoke any arbitrator’s appointment upon its own initiative, at the written
request of all other members of the Arbitral Tribunal or upon a written challenge by any party if: (i)
that arbitrator gives written notice to the LCIA Court of his or her intent to resign as arbitrator, to be
copied to all parties and all other members of the Arbitral Tribunal (if any); (ii) that arbitrator falls
seriously ill, refuses or becomes unable or unfit to act; or (iii) circumstances exist that give rise to
justifiable doubts as to that arbitrator’s impartiality or independence.
10.2 The LCIA Court may determine that an arbitrator is unfit to act under Article 10.1 if that
arbitrator: (i) acts in deliberate violation of the Arbitration Agreement; (ii) does not act fairly or
impartially as between the parties; or (iii) does not conduct or participate in the arbitration with
reasonable efficiency, diligence and industry.
10.3 A party challenging an arbitrator under Article 10.1 shall, within 14 days of the formation of the
Arbitral Tribunal or (if later) within 14 days of becoming aware of any grounds described in Article
10.1 or 10.2, deliver a written statement of the reasons for its challenge to the LCIA Court, the
Arbitral Tribunal and all other parties. A party may challenge an arbitrator whom it has nominated,
or in whose appointment it has participated, only for reasons of which it becomes aware after the
appointment has been made by the LCIA Court.
10.4 The LCIA Court shall provide to those other parties and the challenged arbitrator a reasonable
opportunity to comment on the challenging party’s written statement. The LCIA Court may require
at any time further information and materials from the challenging party, the challenged arbitrator,
other parties and other members of the Arbitral Tribunal (if any).
10.5 If all other parties agree in writing to the challenge within 14 days of receipt of the written
statement, the LCIA Court shall revoke that arbitrator’s appointment (without reasons).
7 See Claimants’ Letter of 25 January 2019, p. 1; Respondents’ Letter of 7 March 2019, p. 1; Partial Final
Award dated 18 March 2019, ¶ 6.
Decision 10 - 10

10.6 Unless the parties so agree or the challenged arbitrator resigns in writing within 14 days of
receipt of the written statement, the LCIA Court shall decide the challenge and, if upheld, shall
revoke that arbitrator’s appointment. The LCIA Court’s decision shall be made in writing, with
reasons; and a copy shall be transmitted by the Registrar to the parties, the challenged arbitrator
and other members of the Arbitral Tribunal (if any). A challenged arbitrator who resigns in writing
prior to the LCIA Court’s decision shall not be considered as having admitted any part of the written
statement.
10.7 The LCIA Court shall determine the amount of fees and expenses (if any) to be paid for the
former arbitrator’s services, as it may consider appropriate in the circumstances. The LCIA Court may
also determine whether, in what amount and to whom any party should pay forthwith the costs of
the challenge; and the LCIA Court may also refer all or any part of such costs to the later decision of
the Arbitral Tribunal and/or the LCIA Court under Article 28.
37. Section 24(1)(a) of the Arbitration Act further provides:
24 Power of court to remove arbitrator.
(1) A party to arbitral proceedings may (upon notice to the other parties, to the arbitrator concerned
and to any other arbitrator) apply to the court to remove an arbitrator on any of the following
grounds –
(a) that circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to his impartiality[.]
. . . .
38. Section 33 of the Arbitration Act includes the general duty of the tribunal to act fairly and
impartially:
33 General duty of the tribunal
(1) The tribunal shall –
(a) act fairly and impartially as between the parties, giving each party a reasonable
opportunity of putting his case and dealing with that of his opponent.
39. The right to be heard by an independent and impartial tribunal is further reinforced by Article 6(1) of
the European Convention on Human Rights, which became part of English law following the passage
of the Human Rights Act 1998.
40. By their allegation that the Sole Arbitrator is biased, the Undersigned understands Claimants to
invoke Article 10.1(iii) of the LCIA Rules, which provides that an arbitrator may be removed where
Decision 10 - 11

“circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to that arbitrator’s impartiality or
independence”. Section 24(1)(a) of the Arbitration Act is framed in similar terms.
41. The Parties agree that under English law, the standard to determine whether there are “justifiable
doubts” as to an arbitrator’s impartiality or independence under the Arbitration Act is “whether the
fair-minded and informed observer, having considered the facts, would conclude that there was a
real possibility that the tribunal was biased”.8
42. Since the standard under the Arbitration Act is similar to the standard under the LCIA Rules (save
that the Act refers only to impartiality and not, as the Rules, also to independence), this case law will
also be taken into account for the purposes of determining the Challenge.
43. Claimants emphasise that the test does not require the proof of actual bias, but only a “real
possibility” that the arbitrator is or was biased.9
44. Respondents, on the other hand, stress that the purpose is to ascertain the position of the “fair-
minded” and “informed” observer rather than the complainant. In this respect, they rely upon Lord
Hope’s formulation in Hellow v Secretary of State for the Home Department:
2. The observer who is fair-minded is the sort of person who always reserves judgment on every
point until she has seen and fully understood both sides of the argument. She is not unduly sensitive
or suspicious . . . Her approach must not be confused with that of the person who has brought the
complaint. The “real possibility” test ensures that there is this measure of detachment. The
assumptions that the complainer makes are not to be attributed to the observer unless they can be
justified objectively.
3. Then there is the attribute that the observer is “informed”. It makes the point that, before she
takes a balanced approach to any information she is given, she will take the trouble to inform herself
on all matters that are relevant.10
45. The Undersigned agrees with the points made by both sides with respect to the applicable test. As is
clear from the wording of the standard, it seeks to determine whether there is a “real possibility” of
bias, as opposed to actual bias.
8 Claimants’ Letter of 25 January 2019, p. 1; Respondents’ Letter of 7 March 2019, ¶ 5; citing Halliburton
Company v Chubb Bermuda Insurance Ltd [2018] 1 W.L.R. 3361.
9 Claimants’ Letter of 25 January 2019, p. 1.
10 Hellow v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2008] 1 WLR 2416, ¶¶ 2-3; see Respondents’
Letter of 7 March 2019, ¶ 6.
Decision 10 - 12

46. Further, the test is an objective one, by reference to the “fair-minded and informed observer”. As
highlighted by Rix J in the case of Laker Airways Incorporated v FLS Aerospace Limited:
The test is thus objective in at least two respects: the court must find that circumstances exist, and
are not merely believed to exist (although I suppose that a belief may itself be a circumstance); and
secondly, those circumstances must justify doubts as to impartiality. An unjustifiable or perhaps
unreasonable doubt is not sufficient . . .11
47. The Undersigned also recalls the well-established rule that in case of real ground for doubt, it should
be resolved in favour of recusal.12
48. Taking into account this legal standard, the Undersigned proceeds to examine the substance of the
Challenge, and in particular whether circumstances exist that give rise to justifiable doubts as to the
impartiality or independence of the Sole Arbitrator.
III. ANALYSIS
49. Claimants raise a number of grounds for the Challenge. In the subsections that follow, the
Undersigned will set forth the relevant facts relating to each alleged ground for the Challenge. Under
each ground, the Undersigned will also summarise the Parties’ and the Sole Arbitrator’s respective
positions regarding that ground. For convenience, the analysis of the Undersigned with respect to
the timeliness and merits of each ground is set out after the relevant positions. In addition to this
ground-by-ground analysis, Section 0 below contains an assessment of the grounds of the Challenge
as a whole.
50. The numerous detailed arguments made by the Parties and the Sole Arbitrator have been
considered in reaching the determinations herein. To the extent that an argument from the written
submissions is not referred to expressly, it is subsumed into the Undersigned’s analysis.
Ground 1: Alleged impermissible conflict of interest of the LCIA
51. Claimants assert that the fact that [C], a partner of [Law Firm D] (Respondents’ counsel in these
proceedings) has been appointed President of the LCIA Court as of [a certain date] May 2019,
“creates the appearance of impropriety, if not actual impropriety” in these proceedings.13
11 Laker Airways Incorporated v FLS Aerospace Limited [2000] 1 WLR 113; extracted in Respondents’ Letter
of 7 March 2019.
12 Locabail (UK) v. Bayfield Properties Ltd [2000] 1 All ER 65, ¶ 77.
Decision 10 - 13

52. Claimants request the LCIA Court to recuse the Sole Arbitrator and then itself from conducting this
arbitration “because an impartial observer would conclude that the LCIA Court and the Tribunal are
biased against the Claimants”.14 On 5 February 2019, the LCIA declined to recuse itself from
administering the arbitration (see ¶ 18 above).
53. The Undersigned is deciding upon the Challenge to the Sole Arbitrator pursuant to Article 10 of the
LCIA Rules. Article 10 empowers the LCIA Court to revoke an arbitrator’s appointment in certain
circumstances (see the full provision extracted at ¶ 36 above). The Undersigned is not competent to
revoke the LCIA’s mandate to administer these proceedings, as Claimants acknowledge.15
54. In this Decision, the Undersigned will therefore confine his analysis to the question of whether the
revocation of the Sole Arbitrator’s appointment is warranted, pursuant to the LCIA Rules and English
law. The Undersigned will consider the circumstances and allegations made against the LCIA Court
only insofar as Claimants allege that the Sole Arbitrator’s appointment is “tainted” by the alleged
bias of the LCIA Court, giving the appearance that the Sole Arbitrator himself is biased (or is actually
biased).
(a) Claimants’ Position
55. According to Claimants, the Sole Arbitrator exhibits an appearance of bias and actually is biased, as a
result of being appointed by an institution that is permeated by an inherent and impermissible
conflict of interest.16
56. Claimants argue that the fact that the international arbitration community has always tolerated
large firms having influence over the arbitral bodies before which these firms represent parties is not
a valid argument.17 In this respect, Claimants submit that “slavery, segregation, colonization and
13 Claimants’ Letter of 15 January 2019, p. 4.
14 Claimants’ Letter of 25 January 2019, pp. 1-2.
15 In their email of 1 March 2019 to the Undersigned, Claimants state that “[t]he Claimants have raised
other issues regarding the arbitral institution that is administering this arbitration, but the Claimants
understand that such issues do not fall within the scope of your mandate. (The LCIA has already stated that
there is no mechanism for recusal of the LCIA as the administrator of the arbitration).”
16 Claimants’ Letter of 21 March 2019, p. 1.
17 Claimants’ Letter of 21 March 2019, p. 3.
Decision 10 - 14

pillaging of nations, and oppression of women and minorities” were all done improperly and
unlawfully for hundreds of years before necessary change came about.18
57. Claimants’ argument is based upon the fact that Respondents are represented by [Law Firm D] in
these proceedings. Claimants allege that Respondents failed to disclose that [C] is currently Vice
President of the LCIA Court, and as of May 2019 will take over as President of the LCIA Court.
Claimants contend that the President and Vice Presidents of the LCIA Court, as well as the members
of the LCIA Board, have the power to make many vital decisions in the arbitration, creating the
appearance of undue influence over the LCIA institution and Court.19
58. Claimants submit that [C] had access to [Law Firm D’s] files, and may have participated in the
representation of Respondents. This includes (i) accusing Second Claimant of fraud; (ii) making
